As pragmatic people, they find it difficult to worship abstract, legendary, invisible entities, but they readily admire local examples of success, bravery, adventure, and intelligence. This admiration involves complex elements: rational and irrational, emotional and unemotional, conscious and unconscious. The process of sanctification does not elevate individuals as much as it sanctifies a spirit. This spirit forms a cultural tradition and becomes part of the society’s genetic fabric. Continuous sanctification reinforces it.
Sometimes, humans do not control technology; technology controls humans. To surpass Americans, one must do one thing: surpass them in science and technology

Americans have enjoyed superiority for a long time, roughly since World War I. Over seventy years have passed, encompassing several generations; those born after World War II are now over forty years old. This generation has grown up immersed in the idea of "America first," creating a psychological set. Consequently, Americans have become a people who cannot tolerate losing. Technological superiority has gradually developed into national superiority, making it inconceivable to Americans that another people could surpass them.

In my view, the most important force is that people's desires for better lives can only be fulfilled through diligent work. This mechanism emerges from two principles: First, rising living standards depend primarily on increased income and money, which becomes essential for maintaining and improving one's life. Second, most jobs are provided by the private sector; both public and private sectors possess full hiring discretion without lifetime employment. People must work to survive or live better.

Why did sexual liberation emerge post-1960s, not earlier? Is there a logical link with advanced material production? Likely so. Freud suggested civilization inevitably represses human instincts. Marcuse termed this "necessary repression." However, once material prosperity reduces the need for constant effort to survive physically, human instincts emerge freely. Material advances trigger moral revolutions, presenting new societal management challenges— shifting from material production management to human behavioral management. Any society reaching sufficient material wealth encounters this challenge.

Working individuals seem to struggle to find mechanisms for eliminating loneliness. Work is purely technical or material activity, lacking emotional or spiritual exchange. Of course, this doesn't mean such exchanges never occur in workplaces, but establishing them is difficult. American individualism often manifests itself in work settings, creating the greatest obstacle to emotional and spiritual communication.

In what sense are Americans lonely? This question defies a simple answer. One could say America's economic system generates loneliness—society’s emphasis on money transforms relationships into monetary transactions, suppressing human affection. A small gesture of warmth may carry monetary implications.

Another perspective argues Americans’ protection of privacy simultaneously protects loneliness; people prefer others not to invade their private lives. This desire fosters loneliness. Perhaps Americans enjoy solitude, or more accurately, prefer moderate solitude. The question is whether they are prepared to handle greater, socially imposed loneliness. Mechanisms individuals design and establish to ensure moderate solitude collectively impose unbearable loneliness upon them. Issues these mechanisms create for individuals become latent social problems. Human loneliness is thus a product of social systems; as long as these systems persist, solutions are elusive. The most challenging aspect of any system is overcoming its own byproducts.

After World War II, America became the foremost superpower. Decades of supremacy fostered a strong psychological mindset among Americans: "We are number one." Maintaining this status became a shared national consensus. To retain its leading role in today's fiercely competitive world, America naturally embraced futurism; otherwise, it would fall behind. The "world’s number one" mindset subtly promotes futurism—difficult to pinpoint precisely. However, if a country occupies the world’s top position without constantly striving to surpass others and lead globally, it will naturally be overtaken.

Employment, social life, marriage, education—none guarantee lifelong security under the American system. Government rarely offers permanent protection; even social security requires employment. Individuals can't rely entirely on family, parents, friends, private companies, or even the government. People can only hope for a future society better—or at least not worse—than the present, providing better or at least comparable living conditions. For individuals, future uncertainty strongly motivates belief in futurism.

Most things rich people can do, others can also do once they have money. This is what Marcuse called assimilation or integration. Marcuse criticized this mechanism, believing it assimilates class distinctions, causing the working class to become unconsciously integrated into the capitalist system that exploits them. This is a result of a highly developed commodity economy

Abundant commodities mitigate social conflicts. In fact, commodity shortages provoke conflicts in many societies. Ordinary people seldom ponder profound and intricate problems, instead thinking about their own daily needs. Social harmony is maintained not by meticulously interpreting grand theories, but by meeting people's daily needs.

Abstractly, interpersonal relationships among Americans aren't so complicated, but interactions between people also aren't particularly deep. The core of American life is protecting one's private domain. Thus, few people enjoy others intruding too deeply into their lives or intruding too much into others’ lives.

The overall economy is similar: because all economic sectors compete, the "invisible hand" becomes effective. If the macro environment is not competitive, a few enterprises cannot compete effectively; the "invisible hand" becomes too weak, and the "visible hand" dominates. A competitive economy develops gradually, not overnight. American society developed this mechanism gradually over several centuries.

Forming this mechanism holds great significance for political and administrative systems, greatly relieving them of heavy management burdens. Transportation, communications, daily commodities, real estate, and food are mostly managed by private enterprises through competition. Government’s role involves indirect regulation. Under this condition, the "invisible hand" reduces governmental burdens, while the "visible hand" increases them.

A developed commodity economy makes everyone equal before money: having money means being able to buy anything purchasable, with no set boundaries. Money is the tangible driving force behind capitalist social development; pursuing money fuels economic and social progress.

Money becomes a fundamental medium of social control. People manage money, and simultaneously, money manages people. A comprehensive system centered on money constitutes an important mechanism in American social management. People serve money. Due to the vital status of money, individuals exhaust their creativity to devise various mechanisms, methods, and techniques for managing money. Consequently, a vast managerial system emerges with money as its medium. Capital utilizes precisely this system to extract surplus value.

Marx said that under capitalism, commodity economies appear as relationships between objects but are, in fact, relationships between people. This profound insight applies universally to interpersonal relations represented through object relations. Managing money is effectively managing people. This nongovernmental monetary mechanism regulates people's thoughts, feelings, and behaviors.

the Constitution is culture, not just law. For over two centuries, the Constitution has deeply influenced people's hearts, becoming the ultimate arbiter of social disputes. People don’t always think about the Constitution, but when conflicts arise, the only universally trusted recourse is the Constitution.

Technological progress promoted regulatory society. Advanced technology entering homes compelled compliance with necessary rules—otherwise, benefits remain inaccessible, or dangers arise. Faster cars require strict rules to avoid fatalities; developed highways necessitate rule adherence. Televisions, recorders, cameras, washing machines, rice cookers, microwaves, audio systems, vacuum cleaners, lawnmowers, mixers, slicers, letter-openers, canopeners, massagers, electric toothbrushes, razors, video games—all demand understanding more complex rules than natural tools. Technology—computers, laser printers, fax machines, copiers—refuses operation without rule compliance.

Americans grow up surrounded by rule adherence through societal compulsion. Entering society means accepting rules. It becomes lifestyle and culture, cultivating habitual rule-following. A striking comparison: Americans cook strictly following recipes and measurements, while Chinese rarely consult recipes, relying instead on estimation. Technological advancement creates specialized products demanding rule-following.

At minimum, Americans clearly understand one idea: government spending is funded by their taxes, motivating them to monitor governmental actions closely. Without a taxation system, citizens wouldn't be as invested in government policies, as the connection to personal interests wouldn't feel direct—even if it existed in reality. Taxation serves as a cornerstone of Western political systems. By contributing financially, citizens feel responsible for overseeing government actions. Officials must regularly explain policies to show responsible spending. Voters closely engage with elections, as elected officials directly influence personal interests—whether president, senators,
representatives, governors, state legislators, or local officials. Taxation creates a "contractual" relationship between citizens and officials, fostering accountability—even if passively. In societies without direct taxation, governments still spend money but through different channels, reducing citizens' sense of government accountability.

Here lies a paradox: normal functioning of society—particularly large societies—requires effective cooperation and collective action among members, yet the value people pursue is supremacy of the individual and private domains.

highly advanced science and technology require finer divisions of labor, assigning clear tasks to every individual, thus technically guaranteeing the values of individualism. Automation and computerization enable individuals to perform specific tasks independently, without needing to depend upon others or obey human commands—only machines. This is precisely what Marcuse analyzed as an aspect of human alienation. Science and technology, especially high-tech, must be divided into countless small, specialized tasks for implementation in production processes, each requiring specialists. Even though these roles may seem minor, an untrained person finds them difficult to fill. The higher the technology, the truer this becomes. In the seventeenth century, craftsmen could create an entire product alone; today, circumstances have completely changed.

In societies with highly advanced technology, the level of social organization is generally higher. Conversely, in regions where high-tech or technological development is lacking, the level of social organization and rationalization tends to be lower. In American society, large corporations and enterprises, embodying technological logic, shoulder a significant part of social organizational functions. In economically less-developed societies, one often sees peculiar phenomena: in fields or places where advanced technology is implemented, the degree of organization significantly surpasses the general social level.

Galbraith's idea is that technological development inevitably leads to greater social organization. Economic and technological systems will be managed by professional managers who control entire systems. Galbraith terms this "technostructure." The end result of technological development is that certain people automatically assume the function of managing others—a non-political management significantly reducing political systems' burdens. A primary function of political systems is coordinating behavior. If a mechanism can constrain behavior within rational bounds, society becomes easier to govern.

The technological governance of people emerges entirely unintentionally, like planting flowers deliberately that never bloom, yet inadvertently planting willows that flourish. Advocates initially employing technology did not explicitly envision it becoming a means to manage people, but now technological applications constitute one of society’s strongest mechanisms for managing people. To a significant extent, American society is governed by technological processes. People obey technology more readily than politics. Technological development breaks society into interconnected, minuscule domains, each occupied by individuals.

Radicals criticize this phenomenon as alienation, valid from a human perspective. Yet no society can do without technology, whose logic inevitably unfolds this way. Emphasizing technology, revering technology, and applying technology obviously transcends purely productive, economic, or technical issues. Consequently, while developing technology, one must consider complex issues. Everything has positive and negative dimensions—the critical factor lies in selecting under appropriate historical conditions and finding effective ways to balance these choices.

Americans, by nature, like to argue. Where regulations are unclear, disputes tend to arise. Many factors produce this characteristic. American historical development illustrates why this trait exists: in developing vast, ownerless lands, anyone could claim something as their own. Without disputes or willingness to argue, one would be left with nothing.

neither party possesses a coherent ideology. While there are disagreements between the two parties on numerous issues, within each party, one finds left-wing, right-wing, and centrist views. Party members freely express a broad range of views. Senators or representatives elected on a party ticket can independently choose their positions and may even oppose their party’s proposals.

If one tries to find a definitive Democratic or Republican party platform, it simply doesn't exist. Generally, the parties only have two types of documents stating their positions and views: one is the platform established at nomination conventions, which does not bind anyone, and the other consists of presidential speeches. Hence, neither party clearly articulates their ultimate goals. Instead, they propose reforms on domestic and foreign policies only during elections, not based on any consistent, fundamental guidelines.

tight-knit political organizations and multi-decade platforms are culturally incompatible with American pragmatism. Americans prefer solving immediate issues rather than deep ideological engagements, driven by lifelong individualism, rarely prioritizing political organizations over personal interests. Americans choose political affiliations based on self-interest.

both parties' open-door policies impose no real disciplinary constraints on grassroots members, promoting inclusivity. Though derogatively termed a "hodgepodge," this inclusiveness helps parties maintain longevity. With unclear boundaries and unrestricted entry or exit, opposing these parties becomes meaningless. Ordinary citizens can only create disturbances since true power rests with small groups of leaders beyond common reach.
Because interest groups influence decision-making, politics become pluralistic. If there were no forces in society capable of influencing government decision-making, politics would become unitary.

Does strict democracy correspond with the developmental laws or intrinsic requirements of large-scale societies? Americans theoretically advocate democratic governance and constitutional democracy, yet psychologically and culturally revere elites. Few nations idolize elites as Americans do. Although Americans outwardly appear indifferent toward many things, their culture deeply embraces hero worship, likely tied to American history and national development. This psychology and cultural value underpin elite governance in America. Conceptually, Americans support mass democracy; practically, they accept elite governance (see Chapter 3, Section 4, "Sanctification").

The establishment of capitalism in the colonies meant commodity production and exchange attained dominance. The logic of commodity production naturally creates demands for democracy: commodity values derive from uniform abstract labor—only through qualitative equivalence can commodities exchange. Commodities exchange according to equal value, measured by socially necessary labor time, spontaneously calculated under average production conditions, average skill levels, and average labor intensity. These conditions themselves imply equality, meaning producers are socially equal. A democratic republic institutionalizes this economic principle—“commodities are natural-born egalitarians”—politically and legally.

Thus, formal democratization coincides with substantive centralization.
This scenario inevitably results in citizens formally enjoying broader democratic rights to participate in production and public management. Substantively, however, their democratic activities consciously serve capital concentration. Actions unify under a singular intention. Frankfurt School scholar Herbert Marcuse, analyzing America’s economic-political structure, concluded insightfully: “Private space is invaded and eroded by technological reality. Mass production and distribution demand total possession of the individual.” This process inevitably affects politics, creating unprecedented political unification—a level of control unimaginable to even the most skilled technicians or conductors.

Harvard Professor Daniel Bell stated in 1976: “In Western political systems, the core issue involves tension between wide participation aspirations and bureaucratic realities.” Participatory democracy temporarily resolves this tension by formally expanding participation while strengthening governance—a subtle yet effective method aligned with commodity equality principles. Modern American suffrage, incorporating initiative and referendum, shifts partially from indirect to direct forms, allowing direct popular intervention in previously representative-managed affairs.

Whichever candidate seeks the presidency must propose solutions to these problems. In reality, candidates do not know if these problems can be solved; however, to get elected, they must present plans. These proposals have long existed in society, often in multiple forms. The role of parties is simply to select the most popular or sympathetic solutions and present them as their own. In fact, "select" might not even be an accurate term: from the perspective of political parties, it's about bringing their product—the candidate—to the market; from the voters' perspective, it's shopping among available products in the market.

Thus, elections create a peculiar logic: Is it parties choosing voters or voters choosing parties? Often, it's probably parties choosing voters. Consequently, political parties lack unified platforms; party members may frequently shift allegiances, and voters may switch from left to right at will.

In promoting openness, society possesses two motivating forces: one is the parties aiming to win; the other is the public. In many societies, the demand for openness comes primarily from the public. Material abundance often leads people to overlook abstract political principles, focusing instead on emotional perceptions of candidates. The system encourages this behavior. Anyone seeking political office must secure votes—without votes, nothing else matters. This necessity pushes candidates to maximize their visibility. Candidates travel widely, pose publicly, and appear on TV for precisely this purpose. People felt uneasy about Quayle partly because he appeared too young and inexperienced. Entrusting public affairs to someone perceived as inexperienced caused anxiety. Actually, Americans care little for politics itself—they care about the candidate’s personality. This phenomenon might be called the "depoliticization of politics."

high-level elections like congressional races rarely inspire enthusiasm or motivation. Most people remain indifferent—a key democratic condition, though not ideal. If everyone held strong political interest, democracy might not function smoothly. Some argue democracy’s biggest enemy isn’t autocracy but democracy itself.

Although the presidential selection mechanism was controlled by parties—not accessible to everyone— the final outcome was authentic. The losing party could neither reject reality nor pursue alternatives. Even if someone attempted otherwise, no one would support it.

Generally speaking, the hallmark of a mature political system is the universal belief that procedurally valid outcomes cannot be resolved through nonprocedural means. Only the procedure itself can resolve any disputes. To change outcomes, the entire procedural cycle must repeat from the beginning— timing determined by law. Belief in procedures doesn't aim to constrain oneself but prevent abuses by others. Procedures capable of harming others could equally harm oneself. A maturing system continuously reinforces such psychological and cognitive beliefs while society provides sufficient conditions to sustain and institutionalize them.

Societal management systems and forms should remain flexible rather than rigid. Overly rigid structures limit dynamic social growth. Conversely, excessive flexibility can produce disorderly management without structural coherence. Finding an appropriate balance between these extremes optimizes social management.

There are two basic methods for managing or governing a society: political governance and technical governance, also known as "soft governance." Soft governance refers to society’s development of effective mechanisms for governing through economic, cultural, customary, and legal means. Political governance heavily utilizes power and coercion, thereby increasing burdens and responsibilities for political and administrative systems. If the political and administrative systems can delegate a substantial part of their responsibilities and still effectively manage societal affairs, a mature governance system emerges. Consequently, contradictions and conflicts caused by political governance diminish. The United States is a capitalist society based on private ownership. Through deliberate design and the inherent power of capital, it has developed soft governance methods, significantly contributing to social stability.

In highly developed production societies, however, automation, electrification, and computerization render these rigid rules largely unnecessary, while "soft rules" become crucial. Soft rules primarily coordinate psychological and emotional states. Automated assembly lines force worker compliance. We observed multiple high-speed assembly lines at this factory, imposing
significant workloads—called "dehumanized coercion." Psychologically, "dehumanized coercion" proves more acceptable than personal coercion.

American corporate authoritarianism has become technical and automated, or "rationalized," to borrow Marcuse's terminology. Remaining management tasks involve coordinating people's inner worlds. However, the rationalization of irrationality continually suppresses human souls quietly—a process intensified by modern science and technology. For Western societies, this psychological issue will remain a significant challenge for a long time.

Only after arriving in the U.S., surrounded by hamburgers, hot dogs, and French fries, does one realize that eating dumplings and preserved vegetables feels like a high-level pleasure. Many Chinese people, even after years in America, still aren't accustomed to Western food. Perhaps this is a kind of Chinese "weakness."

America’s management method differs markedly from China’s traditional style. American management emphasizes rigidity and strictness, while traditional Chinese management favors flexibility and human sentiment. Americans naturally consider rigidity self-evident; Chinese believe flexibility is inherently correct.

In capitalist societies, private enterprises pursue their goals by employing various governance methods, while governments primarily regulate these private enterprises. This dual-layered management—society’s self-organized systems and the government's regulatory system—emerges. The government only supervises from above, without becoming entangled in operational details, thus easing its administrative burdens. Society’s self-organized systems follow their own stable rules, procedures, and functions. Political shifts rarely disrupt these well-functioning systems. In pursuing their individual objectives, these corporations inadvertently propel societal operations forward. This mechanism forms the foundation of the political system—specifically, the American political structure. Large American corporations play precisely this dual role.

For any society, the most difficult task is not reproducing commodities or products, but reproducing institutions. Institutional reproduction refers to whether a specific social system can survive through the next generation, and generations after that. The most solid foundation for institutional existence is societal recognition. Whether the new generation accepts a certain institution directly determines if that institution can reproduce itself. The most important mechanism for institutional reproduction is social education. Social education disseminates the values produced by society, thus providing fundamental conditions for the survival of institutions.

Education is a field of greatest controversy and disagreement in any society; conservatism versus progressivism, tradition versus modernity, and theism versus atheism are all reflected here. The views held by board members largely determine the education received by the next generation.

American universities, especially prestigious ones, are truly among the wealthiest institutions. Precisely for this reason, universities play a crucial role in spreading modernization. It can be said that America’s modernization was fostered by its thousands of universities. Young people first encounter and learn modernization in universities, and most importantly, acquire "modern consciousness." If a generation lacks "modern consciousness," they can only enjoy modernization but cannot create it. Universities have ample funding, enabling them to serve as laboratories for modernization. Everyone who enters a university seems to have fallen into a "vat of modernization." Thus, upon graduation, they are imprinted with an indelible "modern consciousness."

The management quality of a society closely relates to the competence of its government officials. A highly efficient public management system cannot form without qualified and capable government officials; it lacks the necessary conditions. Conversely, a rigorously trained civil service provides a foundation for efficient public management. Public management is inseparable from its civil service system, and civil service relies heavily on government talent development, as the system doesn't merely recruit the best individuals, but those with the greatest managerial talent. Civil service examinations alone cannot guarantee government efficiency; managerial competence isn't innate. Rigorous educational training is essential to cultivating such talent. Training specialized government personnel directly influences the quality of political and administrative systems, significantly impacting comprehensive socioeconomic development.

By what means does a society spread its dominant lifestyle? Throughout history, various methods can be identified, such as military conquest—like the Roman Empire conquering provinces, or Fascists conquering neighboring countries; or political relationships—such as between colonial powers and colonies; economic integration—like today's global system, international trade, and large-scale financial exchanges; educational infiltration—as in the era of Hellenization or medieval theological dominance. Among these methods, military conquest is coercive, political relationships involve power; neither guarantees that a set of values truly penetrates people's hearts. They can enforce a certain ideology, but can't make people sincerely accept and abide by it.

In today’s world, the latter two methods dominate. One is economic power. The development of economic strength reveals people's fundamental nature and pursuits, making it easy to accept. America’s post-war economic growth has become the primary vehicle for spreading its lifestyle. The second is educational power. Education is a magical force; it subtly spreads a society's dominant beliefs. This is true both internally within a society, and externally in its relations with others.

Educational exports significantly influence people's ways of thinking, emotional orientation, psychological patterns, value choices, and codes of conduct. Many of those educated here become elite figures in their countries, playing critical roles in politics, economics, culture, education, technology, and arts. Educational exports serve two primary functions: knowledge dissemination and emotional investment. The latter is political capital that no country can underestimate.

Pressure on a political system can originate internally or externally. If external forces approve and endorse a political system’s activities and choices, internal pressures decrease significantly. External affirmation neutralizes internal negativity. If a political system faces strong external opposition or misunderstanding, internal pressures increase, causing difficulties.

Think tanks intentionally or unintentionally serve as "social doctors." They continually identify societal problems, proposing solutions, conditions necessary for their survival and securing funding. To obtain financial support, they must be innovative or original, motivating them to uncover policy issues.

The development of a society is inseparably linked to the dissemination of knowledge, especially advanced knowledge. Summarizing the history of human development, the emergence of new knowledge or wisdom often does not necessarily imply social progress; rather, it is the wide dissemination of this new knowledge or wisdom that indicates social progress. Without a mechanism for dissemination, new knowledge or wisdom cannot become a powerful force driving social advancement.

Libraries are open reservoirs of knowledge where everyone can swim freely. Social progress depends on individuals’ ability to access and master the knowledge accumulated and created by society. To maximally achieve this goal, everyone must be able to quickly and easily access knowledge and ideas,

Maximizing openness is essential for libraries to deliver maximum benefit. Without this condition, reservoirs become stagnant, losing their societal effectiveness. Reservoirs are built not to store water but to irrigate. Knowledge reservoirs are the same.

Managing any society, to a large extent, involves managing knowledge. Whether political, administrative, economic, or technical management, ultimately it is human management. People aren't abstract, mechanical objects; they possess thoughts and independent judgment. Human behavior is primarily driven by ideas—established culture, existing concepts, and the innovations built upon these foundations. All social progress and conflict fundamentally stem from knowledge management.

History teaches us that a primary responsibility of political systems is knowledge management. Knowledge determines the level of political development. In a sense, knowledge structures can either lead to political progress or political decline. Historically, every political leap forward—or transition between old and new politics—is closely tied to knowledge advancement or stagnation.

American society employs decentralized knowledge management. Naturally, no knowledge management can be entirely depoliticized. Yet societal knowledge management is largely independent from administrative systems. The administrative system formally does not carry this heavy responsibility. The highly developed library system allows this method to function effectively. In societies where knowledge dissemination systems are poorly organized, administrative systems bear an exceedingly heavy burden of knowledge dissemination—not only to spread knowledge but also to establish a solid foundation for the administrative system itself. Highly organized, welldeveloped knowledge dissemination systems clearly have profound implications for social and political management.

In a commodity-driven economy, monetary power is irresistible. Without guidance, profit becomes people's sole focus, leading eventually to severe social problems. Many developing nations face this dilemma. Economic growth initially mobilizes monetary mechanisms, channeling people's energies. Once growth necessitates high technology and advanced skills, suitable talent becomes scarce, as monetary incentives drive people toward simple, immediate-earning jobs instead of complex tasks.

The entire mess today arises from a subjectivity that is ignorant of itself, that mistakes itself for objectivity. The idea of the good that is tacitly assumed in the theory stems from the fact that thought necessarily includes the element of reflection. This cushions the effect of our actions. Just as the imagination developed out of the age-old misdeeds of biology among other things, helping to strip them of their demonic aspect, in the same way theory contains an anti-mythological dimension. This means that because we pause to reflect we do not just lash out blindly. A person who thinks does not just react with his fists, does not just devour things unthinkingly. The time lag caused by the moment of reflection between hunger, fury and lashing out is the origin of the idea that all will be well. By confronting the ends with the means something necessarily comes into being that brings about the suspension of the entire blindness and immediacy. For me to master nature, I have to think. But by thinking, I interpose a medium between the object of action and myself that strives to go beyond both. The gesture of the savage who pauses for an instant to reflect whether or not he wishes to eat his prisoner contains teleologically the end of violence.

HORKHEIMER: Work is the key to making sure that ‘all will be well’. But by elevating it to godlike status, it is emptied of meaning. ADORNO: How does it come about that work is regarded as an absolute? Work exists to control the hardships of life, to ensure the reproduction of mankind. The success of labour stands in a problematic relationship to the effort required. It does not necessarily or certainly reproduce the lives of those who work but only of those who induce others to work for them. In order to persuade human beings to work you have to fob them off with the waffle about work as the thing in itself.

How does work come to be an end in itself? This dates back to a time far earlier than capitalism. Initially, I suppose, because society reproduced itself through labour, but then in each individual case the relation between concrete labour and reproduction is opaque. In socially useful labour people have to forget what it is good for. The abstract necessity of labour is expressed in the fact that value is ascribed to labour in itself.

The positive side lies in the teleology that work potentially makes work superfluous; the negative side is that we succumb to the mechanism of reification, in the course of which we forget the best thing of all. That turns a part of the process into an absolute. But it is not an aberration, since without it the whole process wouldn’t function.
People repress their own chaotic drives which might lead them away from work. This is what makes them feel that work is sacred.

Because people have to work so hard, there is a sense in which they spend their spare time obsessively repeating the rituals of the efforts that have been demanded of them. We must not be absolutely opposed to work.
The world is not just mad. It is mad and rational as well.
There are countless fields where technology could be properly applied. The goods made available nowadays are a kind of pseudo-consumer goods; exchange value is substituted for use value.

One can certainly define intelligence. The concept contains a mixture of quite different things. The ability to think in isolation from the subject matter in question, and on the other hand, the insight that comes from a grasp of that subject matter. These two aspects are connected, but the usual concept of intelligence refers simply to the first, while the second, which is what counts, is dragged along under the label of intuition or the like. It must be said that formal intelligence is the necessary but not sufficient attribute, and that intuition is only a type of experience that is suddenly activated, and is by no means irrational.

Theory is theory in the authentic sense only where it serves practice. Theory that wishes to be sufficient unto itself is bad theory. On the other hand, it is also bad theory if it exists only in order to produce something or other.

The fact that thinking gives us pleasure is not what justifies the privileging of theory over practice. Where there is no link to practice, thinking is no different from anything else one happens to enjoy. The difference between thinking we approve of and disapprove of is that the thinking we approve of must have a connection to a world set to rights and must look at the world from this perspective. It must relate to the question of how the world is to be made different. If we wish to write about theory and practice we must give a more incisive account of this aspect. Sometimes by practice we mean the fact that everything we think and do should be classified under the heading of change. At other times, we mean by practice whatever relates to the difference between thinking and doing. We must make every effort to ensure that all our thoughts and actions fit in with the first mentioned concept of practice.
What makes theory more than a mere instrument of practice is the fact that it reflects on itself, and in so doing it rescinds itself as mere theory.

In the workers’ movement, there persist longstanding conflicts between individual and collective interests. The attempt to absorb the satisfaction of universal interests into the limited satisfaction of particular interests has to be countered, among other things, by showing that in the long run individual interests can only be appropriately taken into consideration through the satisfaction of universal interests—which means through actual change. Stressing this point of view in opposition to immediate interests often appears [256] ideal, theoretical. But in practical politics too, just as much as in theory, it has to be shown that particular interests are at least as abstract, ephemeral, and ideal as so-called spiritual interests.

books.title: Scaling People: Tactics for Management and Company Building
books.author: Claire Hughes Johnson

highlights.text: “You know why playing a game is fun? Because it has rules, and you have a way to win. Picture a bunch of people showing up at an athletic field with random equipment and no rules. Someone is going to get hurt. You don’t know how to play, you don’t know how to score, and you don’t know how to win.” It’s critical for companies and teams to establish the playing field on which everyone participates and marks progress.

Company-wide frameworks are indicators of your company’s priorities. Think of them as the set of actions or processes that everyone must perform or follow in concert and in the same way. The Mandalorian mantra “This is the way” comes to mind. It’s my belief that the most successful and enduring companies foster strong internal adherence to their core frameworks.

There are massive coordination costs to company-wide processes, and if you impose too many, chances are your employees and managers will devote their time and headspace to following your processes instead of developing new ideas and getting work done. The benefits of uniformity must also outweigh the benefits of variability, and there aren’t too many structures that, when standardized, benefit the entire company. I believe core, company-wide frameworks should apply in the following areas, each of which has its own chapter in the pages to come: Foundations and planning for goals and resources A comprehensive hiring approach Intentional team development Feedback and performance mechanisms

Self-awareness has three components: understanding your underlying value system, identifying your innate preferences—your work style and decision-making tendencies—and being clear about your own skills and capability gaps.

Understanding what is important to you will help you make sense of how you work, what gives you energy and what saps it, and what might trigger an outsize reaction. With those insights, you’ll be able to express your values and understand when they are at odds with one another or with someone else’s values.

Technical problems have a solution and an achievable resolution, while adaptive problems are continuously, well, adapting. They’re an infinite game, if you will.16 A technical problem might be that you consistently miss your customer service-level agreement of responding to an inquiry within two hours. An adaptive problem might be how to set product priorities in the face of evolving user needs and increasing competition. Managers are superb at solving technical problems. Tackling adaptive problems takes leadership.

Leadership is disappointing people at a rate they can absorb. Leadership is ultimately about driving change, while management is about creating stability. Stability is important in a work environment, but confronting challenges and realizing new ideas require discomfort. This means that you and your teams must abandon the stable and familiar in favor of an uncertain—but exciting—new direction.

Experienced employees mostly need a leader and just a bit of a manager. If they’ve made it to a certain point in their careers, they’re probably good at getting their work done. But they’ll look to a leader to lay out the overarching vision and the milestones they should be working toward, and to pave the way for progress within the systems that operate outside of the team. The leader pushes their team to think and act differently, to welcome change, and, ultimately, to aspire to and achieve more ambitious outcomes. Less experienced employees mostly need a manager and just a bit of a leader. They’ll benefit from someone who can help them think through tactics, manage their work and their day-to-day, and help them develop and operate.

The art of planning is to allocate enough funds and employees to earlier-stage efforts to give them a chance to demonstrate success, while simultaneously streamlining the more mature parts of the business so that they realize operational efficiencies and demonstrate increasing profitability as early as possible, without undermining their growth.

Your role as a manager is to make sure your team is defining goals and accomplishing them, but not at the expense of their future ability to do so. When a company is growing, it needs to have a consistent ability to get work done—sustainably—or else growth will stall.

A Code Yellow is a special operating mode intended to increase execution speed and reduce execution risk around a given project. In theory, it can be applied to achieve any aim, but we will use it most often when we must urgently address a substantial risk to our business. A group is assembled and endowed with special powers and privileges to accomplish its goal.

The Code Yellow team will: Be shielded from other organizational obligations. This includes other projects they’re staffed on, as well as things like interviews and spin-ups. Be resourced quickly and aggressively. Staffing will generally be cross-functional and will often entail painful trade-offs against other projects. Have daily standups and write up frequent situation reports (typically daily) on progress and priorities. Have a dedicated physical space (optional but encouraged). Have the power to convene the leadership team to make decisions with a 24-hour response time SLA (service-level agreement). Typically work longer hours than the average team, including longer hours on weekends when needed. Update the company on active Code Yellows at every all-hands meeting.

Compassionate management does not mean holding off on giving feedback because you notice the employee is already overwhelmed or prone to taking feedback badly. It also doesn’t mean dropping your other work to get the person back on track. Compassionate management means providing someone with honest observations of their performance, being clear about the options an employee has to course-correct, outlining what work would be required for them to start meeting expectations, and sharing what you think is the likeliest outcome for them at your organization. It also means balancing all of this feedback with your other responsibilities.

In performance management, timing is everything. Ideally, it takes no more than three months to reach a resolution for any given performance issue. In many cases, issues can be resolved in one month, depending on the employee’s seniority and the context. You don’t want to let issues linger, but you also want to give the person a fair chance to improve.

Every time someone compliments a strength of yours, think about the flip side that might be a weakness. One of mine is that I’m quite strong at operating independently, but that leads me to fall into two traps. The first is that I see work that needs to be done, add it to my plate, then become resentful of colleagues who are not helping, somehow expecting them to be mind readers. The second is that I rarely seek input from peers, even when I’m not the person best suited to a task. Being aware of the flip-side weakness should make you even more effective at using your strength. In my case, communicating when I think help is needed, including for myself, and being more intentional about who takes on which tasks, means I can play more to my strengths.

Ask for help. Management is not just about building a complementary team but also about having the mutual self-awareness to look at your entire orbit and seek out those with different strengths. You can’t go far together unless you’re not just self-aware but also confident enough to be vulnerable and seek others’ assistance.

books.title: The Expulsion of the Other: Society, Perception and Communication Today
books.author: Byung-Chul Han

highlights.text: The negativity of the Other now gives way to the positivity of the Same. The proliferation of the Same constitutes the pathological changes that afflict the social body. It is made sick not by denial and prohibition, but by over-communication and over-consumption; not by suppression and negation, but by permissiveness and affirmation. The pathological sign of our times is not repression but depression. Destructive pressure comes not from the Other but from within.

The violence of the Same is invisible because of its positivity. The proliferation of the Same presents itself as growth. At a certain point, however, production is no longer productive but destructive, information is no longer informative but deformative, and communication is no longer communicative but merely cumulative.

Binge-watching can be generalized as the contemporary mode of perception. The proliferation of the Same resembles not a carcinoma but a coma, and does not meet with any immunological defences. One goggles oneself into unconsciousness.

One travels everywhere, yet does not experience anything. One catches sight of everything, yet reaches no insight. One accumulates information and data, yet does not attain knowledge. One lusts after adventures and stimulation, but always remains the same. One accumulates online ‘friends’ and ‘followers’, yet never encounters another person. Social media constitutes an absolute zero grade of the social.

Total interconnection and total communication by digital means does not facilitate encounters with Others. Rather, it serves to pass over those who are unfamiliar and other, and instead find those who are the same or like-minded, ensuring that our horizon of experience becomes ever narrower. It draws us into an endless ego loop, ultimately leading to an ‘autopropaganda, indoctrinating us with our own ideas’.

Information is simply available. Knowledge in an emphatic sense, however, is a long and slow process. It displays an entirely different temporality. It matures. Maturation is a temporality that we are increasingly losing today. It is not compatible with today’s politics of time, which fragments time and eliminates temporally stable structures in order to increase efficiency and productivity.

A correlation states: when A occurs, B often also occurs. It is not known, however, why this is so. Correlation is the most primitive form of knowledge, being not even capable of ascertaining the relationship between cause and effect. It is so. The question of why becomes irrelevant; thus nothing is understood. But knowledge is understanding.

Digital gaplessness removes all varieties of proximity and distance. Everything is equally near and equally far: ‘Trace and aura. The trace is appearance of a nearness, however far removed the thing that left it may be. The aura is appearance of a distance, however close the thing that calls it forth.’

Globalization has an inherent violence that makes everything interchangeable, comparable and thus the same. Ultimately, this total equalization leads to a negation of meaning; meaning is something incomparable.1 Yet money creates neither meaning nor identity. The violence of the global as the violence of the Same destroys the negativity of the Other, of the singular, of the incomparable, which impairs the circulation of information, communication and capital. It is precisely where the Same encounters the Same that this circulation reaches its highest velocity.

the idea of hospitality also displays something universal. For Nietzsche, it is an expression of the ‘over-abundant soul’. It is capable of harbouring all singularities within itself: ‘And let all that is becoming roaming searching fleeing be welcome here! Henceforth the friendship of hospitality will be my only friendship.’15 Hospitality promises reconciliation. Its aesthetic manifestation is beauty: ‘We are always rewarded in the end for our good will, our patience, our fair-mindedness and gentleness with what is strange, as it gradually casts off its veil and presents itself as a new and indescribable beauty. That is its thanks for our hospitality.’16 The politics of beauty is the politics of hospitality. Xenophobia is hatred, and ugly. It is an expression of a lack of universal reason, a sign that society is still in an unreconciled state. How civilized a society is can be judged by its hospitality in particular, indeed its friendliness. Reconciliation means friendliness.

Fear results when there is no longer any object charged with libido. The world thus becomes empty and senseless. Owing to the lack of object attachment, the ego is thrown back on itself and broken by itself. Depression is attributable to a narcissistic accumulation of ego-libido.

Today’s culture of performance and optimization does not allow us to work through conflicts, which is time-consuming. Today’s performance subject only knows two states: functioning or failing. In this, there is a resemblance to the condition of machines: machines also know no conflict. They either function correctly or are broken. Conflicts are not destructive; they have a constructive side. It is only from conflicts that stable relationships and identities ensue. A person grows and matures by working through conflict.

What dominates today is not the uniformity of ‘every Other is like the next’ that characterizes the ‘they’. That uniformity gives way to the diversity of opinions and options. Diversity only permits differences that conform to the system; it constitutes an otherness that has been made consumable. And it perpetuates the Same more efficiently than uniformity does, for its apparent, superficial variety obscures the systemic violence of the Same. Variety and different options create the illusion of an otherness that, in reality, does not exist.

For Heidegger, anxiety is closely connected to death. Death is not simply the end of Being, but rather ‘a way to be’,5 namely the outstanding possibility to be the self. Dying means: ‘“I am,” which means that I will be my ownmost I.’6 In the face of death, a ‘reticent resoluteness that exacts anxiety of itself’7 chooses eigentlich self-Being. Death is my death.

In our time, which strives to banish all negativity from life, death too falls silent. It no longer speaks. It is deprived of all language. It is no longer ‘a way to be’, but rather no more than the mere end of life, which must be delayed by all means. Death simply means de-production, the end of production.

It is precisely negativity that enlivens. It nourishes the life of the spirit. The spirit only gains its truth when, in utter fragmentation, it finds itself. Only the negativity of rupture and pain keeps the spirit alive. The spirit ‘is this power, not as something positive which closes its eyes to the negative’; it is this power ‘only by looking the negative in the face, and dwelling on it’.10 Today, we flee desperately from the negative instead of dwelling on it. Holding on to the positive, however, only reproduces the Same. There is not only a hell of negativity, but also a hell of positivity. Terror originates not only from the negative, but also from the positive.

We live today in the neoliberal system, which breaks down temporally stable structures, fragments living-time and permits the disintegration of what binds us together in the interests of increasing productivity. This neoliberal politics of time creates anxiety and insecurity. And neoliberalism fragments humans into isolated entrepreneurs of themselves. This isolation, which goes hand in hand with the elimination of solidarity and total competition, produces anxiety. The diabolical logic of neoliberalism is this: anxiety increases productivity.

Anxiety also awakens on the threshold; it is a typical threshold feeling. The threshold is a transition to the unknown. Beyond the threshold, a completely different state of being begins. Thus death is always inscribed in the threshold. In all rites of passages, one dies a death in order to be reborn beyond the threshold. Here death is experienced as a transition: whoever crosses the boundary subjects themselves to a transformation. As a place of transformation, the threshold hurts.

The compulsion to accelerate the global circulation of capital, communication and information breaks thresholds down and results in a threshold-less, smooth space with an extremely accelerated internal rotation. This is where a new anxiety develops, an anxiety that is completely disconnected from the negativity of the Other. Digital communication as a new form of production rigorously abolishes all distance in order to become faster. Every protective distance is thus lost. In hypercommunication, everything is mixed with everything else. The boundaries between inside and outside become increasingly permeable. Today, we are completely deexternalized into a ‘pure surface’, exposed to the incoming rays of all ‘influent networks’.

This forced transparency eliminates every gap of vision and information, handing everything over to complete visibility. It causes all spaces of retreat and protection to disappear; thus everything moves threateningly close to us. There is nothing to shield us. We ourselves become no more than transits amid the global network. Transparency and hypercommunication deprive us of any protective inwardness. Indeed, we relinquish them voluntarily and expose ourselves to digital webs that penetrate, illuminate and perforate us. Digital over-exposure and nakedness create a latent fear that stems not from the negativity of the Other, but rather from the excess of positivity. The transparent hell of sameness is not devoid of fear; what is frightening is precisely the increasingly strong roaring of the Same.

Today we abandon ourselves to a boundless communication. We are almost benumbed by digital hypercommunication. But the noise of communication does not make us any less lonely. Perhaps it even makes us lonelier than speech-grilles do. After all, beyond the speech-grille there is at least a you; it still preserves the closeness of distance. Hypercommunication, however, destroys both the you and closeness. Relationships are replaced by connections. Gaplessness supplants closeness. Two mouthfuls of silence might contain more closeness, more language than hypercommunication. Silence is language, but the noise of communication is not.

Today, we live in a post-Marxist age. In the neoliberal regime, exploitation no longer takes place as alienation and self-derealization, but as freedom, as self-realization and self-optimization. Here there is no Other as an exploiter, forcing me to work and alienating me from myself; rather, I voluntarily exploit myself in the belief that I am realizing myself. This is the diabolical logic of neoliberalism. Hence the first stage of a burnout is euphoria: I plunge into work euphorically until I finally collapse. I realize myself to death. I optimize myself to death. Neoliberal domination hides behind the illusion of freedom. The domination is complete at the moment when it coincides with freedom. This feeling of freedom is disastrous insofar as it does not enable any resistance, any revolution. Where should resistance direct itself? There are no longer any Others from whom any repression originates.

The digital order causes an increasing disembodiment of the world; today, there is less and less communication between bodies. It also does away with counter-bodies by robbing things of their material heaviness, their mass, their own weight, their own life, their own time, and makes them available at all times.

What distinguishes the digital medium from the optical one is that it is a medium with no gaze. So too the digital panopticon, which would in fact no longer be an opticon, does not rely on the gaze, on the central optical perspective. That is precisely why it sees substantially more, and indeed more deeply, than the analogous Panopticon. The distinction between centre and periphery becomes meaningless; the digital panopticon operates aperspectivally. Aperspectival screening is far more efficient than perspectival surveillance because one is illuminated from all sides, even from the inside. Thoughts elude the gaze, but they do not escape the digital panopticon. Big Data has no need for the gaze. Unlike surveillance with a central perspective, aperspectival screening no longer has any blind spots.

Digital means of communication are far more disembodied than letters. Handwriting is still a body sign; all digital writing is the same. Most of all, digital media elide the Other as a counterpart. They actually rob us of the ability to think about someone far away and to hold on to someone nearby. They replace closeness and distance with gaplessness.

Digital communication is highly deficient in gaze and voice. Connections and interconnections are created without the voice or the gaze. In this, they differ from relationships and encounters, which are dependent on the voice and the gaze. They are, in fact, special experiences of the voice and the gaze. They are bodily experiences.

The digital medium has a disembodying effect. It robs the voice of its grain, its corporeality, indeed the depths of the cavities, muscles, membranes and cartilage. The voice is smoothed out. It becomes transparent for meaning. Its only content is the signified.

For Adorno, ‘estrangement from the world’ is an aspect of art. Someone who perceives the world as anything other than foreign is not perceiving it at all. A negative tension is essential to art; for Adorno, there was therefore no such thing as feel-good art. Likewise, estrangement from the world is an aspect of philosophy. It inheres in spirit itself. Thus spirit, by its very nature, is critique.

Today’s hypercommunication suppresses the free spaces of silence and solitude without which it would have been impossible to say things that were truly worth saying. It suppresses language, of which silence is an essential part. It rises from a silence; without that, it is already noise.

To encounter a human being, according to Levinas, ‘is to be kept awake by an enigma’.7 Today, we have lost this experience of the Other as an enigma or secret. The Other now is entirely subject to the teleology of use, to economic calculation and evaluation. They become transparent. They are demoted to an economic object. The Other as an enigma, on the other hand, eludes all exploitation.

Love always presupposes otherness – not only the otherness of the Other, but also the otherness of one’s own person. The duality of the person is constitutive of love for oneself: What is love but understanding and rejoicing at the fact that another lives, acts and feels in a way different from and opposite to ours? If love is to bridge these antitheses through joy it may not deny or seek to abolish them. – Even self-love presupposes an unblendable duality (or multiplicity) in one person.8 When all duality is wiped out, one drowns in the self. Without any duality, one merges with oneself. This narcissistic meltdown is fatal.

Listening is not a passive act. It is distinguished by a special activity: first I must welcome the Other, which means affirming the Other in their otherness. Then I give them an ear. Listening is a bestowal, a giving, a gift. It helps the Other to speak in the first place. It does not passively follow the speech of the Other. In a sense, listening precedes speaking; it is only listening that causes the Other to speak. I am already listening before the Other speaks, or I listen so that the Other will speak. Listening invites the Other to speak; it frees them for their otherness. The listener is a resonance chamber in which the Other speaks themselves free. Thus listening can have a healing effect.

In analogue communication we usually have a concrete addressee, a personal counterpart. Digital communication, on the other hand, fosters an expansive, de-personalized communication that has no need of a personal counterpart, no need of a gaze or a voice. We constantly send messages on Twitter, for example. But they are not directed at a concrete person. They mean no one. Social media do not necessarily foster a culture of discussion. They are often affect-driven. Shitstorms are an undirected flood of affects that does not form any public discourse.

Without the presence of the Other, communication degenerates into an accelerated exchange of information. It creates no relationship, only connection. It is a communication with no neighbour, without any neighbourly closeness. Listening means something entirely different from exchanging information; listening does not involve any exchange whatsoever. Without neighbourliness, without listening, no community can form. Community is listenership.

Listening has a political dimension. It is an act, an active participation in the existence of Others, in their suffering too. It is what joins and connects people to form a community in the first place. Today, we hear a great deal, but are increasingly losing the ability to listen to Others and give an ear to their language, their suffering. Today, everyone is somehow on their own with themselves, with their suffering, with their fears. Suffering is privatized and individualized. Thus it becomes an object of a therapy that tampers with the I, with its psyche. Everyone is ashamed and simply blames themselves for their weakness and inadequacy. No connection is established between my suffering and your suffering. Thus the sociality of suffering is overlooked.

The noisy society of fatigue is deaf. The society to come, by contrast, could be termed a society of listeners and hearkeners. What is needed today is a temporal revolution that ushers in a completely different time; we must rediscover the time of the Other. Today’s temporal crisis is not acceleration, but rather the totalization of the time of the self. The time of the Other eludes the logic of increase based on performance and efficiency, which creates a pressure to accelerate. The neoliberal politics of time does away with the time of the Other, which it considers an unproductive time. The totalization of the time of the self goes hand in hand with the totalization of production, which affects all areas of contemporary life and leads to the total exploitation of humans.

books.title: Psychopolitics: Neoliberalism and New Technologies of Power
books.author: Byung-Chul Han

highlights.text: Freedom will prove to have been merely an interlude. Freedom is felt when passing from one way of living to another – until this too turns out to be a form of coercion. Then, liberation gives way to renewed subjugation.

Today, we do not deem ourselves subjugated subjects, but rather projects: always refashioning and reinventing ourselves. A sense of freedom attends passing from the state of subject to that of project. All the same, this projection amounts to a form of compulsion and constraint – indeed, to a more efficient kind of subjectivation and subjugation. As a project deeming itself free of external and alien limitations, the I is now subjugating itself to internal limitations and self-constraints, which are taking the form of compulsive achievement and optimization.

The freedom of Can generates even more coercion than the disciplinarian Should, which issues commandments and prohibitions. Should has a limit. In contrast, Can has none. Thus, the compulsion entailed by Can is unlimited. And so we find ourselves in a paradoxical situation.
Psychic maladies such as depression and burnout express a profound crisis of freedom. They represent pathological signs that freedom is now switching over into manifold forms of compulsion.

As the entrepreneur of its own self, the neoliberal subject has no capacity for relationships with others that might be free of purpose. Nor do entrepreneurs know what purpose-free friendship would even look like. Originally, being free meant being among friends. ‘Freedom’ and ‘friendship’ have the same root in Indo-European languages. Fundamentally, freedom signifies a relationship. A real feeling of freedom occurs only in a fruitful relationship – when being with others brings happiness. But today’s neoliberal regime leads to utter isolation; as such, it does not really free us at all.

Neoliberalism represents a highly efficient, indeed an intelligent, system for exploiting freedom. Everything that belongs to practices and expressive forms of liberty – emotion, play and communication – comes to be exploited. It is inefficient to exploit people against their will. Allo-exploitation yields scant returns. Only when freedom is exploited are returns maximized.

As a mutant form of capitalism, neoliberalism transforms workers into entrepreneurs. It is not communist revolution that is now abolishing the allo-exploited working class – instead, neoliberalism is in the course of doing so. Today, everyone is an auto-exploiting labourer in his or her own enterprise. People are now master and slave in one. Even class struggle has transformed into an inner struggle against oneself.

In fact, no proletariat exists under the neoliberal regime at all. There is no working class being exploited by those who own the means of production. When production is immaterial, everyone already owns the means of production him- or herself. The neoliberal system is no longer a class system in the proper sense. It does not consist of classes that display mutual antagonism. This is what accounts for the system’s stability.

The neoliberal regime transforms allo-exploitation into auto-exploitation; this process affects all ‘classes’. Such classless self-exploitation – which was something utterly unknown to Marx – renders impossible any social revolution based on the difference between the exploiters, on the one hand, and the exploited, on the other. Indeed, given the auto-exploiting achievement-subject’s isolation, no political We is even possible that could rise up and undertake collective action.
People who fail in the neoliberal achievement-society see themselves as responsible for their lot and feel shame instead of questioning society or the system.

Now, under the neoliberal regime of auto-exploitation, people are turning their aggression against themselves. This auto-aggressivity means that the exploited are not inclined to revolution so much as depression.

In our world, we no longer work in order to satisfy our own needs. Instead, we work for Capital. Capital generates needs of its own; mistakenly, we perceive these needs as if they belonged to us. Capital therefore represents a new kind of transcendence, which entails a new form of subjectivation. We are being expelled from the sphere of lived immanence – where life relates to life instead of subjugating itself to external ends.

Do we really want to be free? Didn’t we invent God so we wouldn’t have to be free? Before God, we are all debtors: guilty (schuldig). But debt – guilt – destroys freedom. Today, politicians appeal to high debt rates to explain that their freedom to act is massively restricted. Free from debt – that is, wholly free – we would truly have to act. Perhaps we run up debts perpetually so we won’t need to do so – that is, so we won’t need to be free, or responsible. Don’t our debts prove that we don’t have the power to be free? Could it be that Capital is a new God, making us guilty and debt-ridden again?

Under the immaterial mode of production that now prevails, more information and more communication mean more productivity, acceleration and growth. Information represents a positive value; inasmuch as it lacks interiority, it can circulate independently, free from any and all context. Accordingly, the circulation of information admits acceleration at will – for purely arbitrary reasons.
The negativity of otherness or foreignness is de-interiorized and transformed into the positivity of communicable and consumable difference: ‘diversity’.

The dispositive of transparency has the further consequence of promoting total conformity. The economy of transparency seeks to suppress deviation. Total networking – total communication – already has a levelling effect per se. Its effect is conformity: it is as if everyone were watching over everyone else – even before intelligence agencies or secret services have stepped in to supervise and steer. Invisible moderators smooth out communication and calibrate it to what is generally understood and accepted. Such primary, intrinsic surveillance proves much more problematic than the secondary, extrinsic surveillance undertaken by secret services and spying agencies.

Neoliberalism makes citizens into consumers. The freedom of the citizen yields to the passivity of the consumer. As consumers, today’s voters have no real interest in politics – in actively shaping the community. They possess neither the will nor the ability to participate in communal, political action. They react only passively to politics: grumbling and complaining, as consumers do about a commodity or service they do not like.

The transparency demanded of politicians today is anything but a political demand. Transparency is not called for in political decision-making processes; no consumer is interested in that. Instead, and above all, the imperative of transparency serves to expose or unmask politicians, to make them an item of scandal. The call for transparency presupposes occupying the position of a shocked spectator. It is not voiced by engaged citizens so much as by passive onlookers. Participation now amounts to grievance and complaint. With that, the society of transparency, inhabited by onlookers and consumers, has given rise to a spectator democracy.

Today, we are entering the age of digital psychopolitics. It means passing from passive surveillance to active steering. As such, it is precipitating a further crisis of freedom: now, free will itself is at stake. Big Data is a highly efficient psychopolitical instrument that makes it possible to achieve comprehensive knowledge of the dynamics of social communication. This knowledge is knowledge for the sake of domination and control (Herrschaftswissen): it facilitates intervention in the psyche and enables influence to take place on a pre-reflexive level.

For human beings to be able to act freely, the future must be open. However, Big Data is making it possible to predict human behaviour. This means that the future is becoming calculable and controllable. Digital psychopolitics transforms the negativity of freely made decisions into the positivity of factual states (Sachverhalte).

Every dispositive – every technology or technique of domination – brings forth characteristic devotional objects that are employed in order to subjugate. Such objects materialize and stabilize dominion. Devotion and related words mean ‘submission’, or ‘obedience’. Smartphones represent digital devotion – indeed, they are the devotional objects of the Digital, period. As a subjectivation-apparatus, the smartphone works like a rosary – which, because of its ready availability, represents a handheld device too. Both the smartphone and the rosary serve the purpose of self-monitoring and control. Power operates more effectively when it delegates surveillance to discrete individuals.

Power that relies on violence does not represent power of the highest order. The mere fact that another will manages to form and turn against the power-holder attests to the latter’s weakness. Wherever power does not come into view at all, it exists without question. The greater power is, the more quietly it works. It just happens: it has no need to draw attention to itself.

Power need not exclude, prohibit or censor. Not does it stand opposed to freedom. Indeed, power can even use freedom to its own ends. Only in its negative form does power manifest itself as a violence that says ‘no’ by shattering the will and annulling freedom. Today, power is assuming increasingly permissive forms. In its permissivity – indeed, in its friendliness – power is shedding its negativity and presenting itself as freedom.

The neoliberal regime’s technology of power takes on subtle, supple and smart forms; thereby, it escapes all visibility. Now, the subjugated subject is not even aware of its own subjugation. The whole context of domination (Herrschaftszusammenhang) remains entirely hidden. Consequently, the subject thinks itself free.

A significantly more efficient technology of power makes sure that people subordinate themselves to power relations on their own. Such a dynamic seeks to activate, motivate and optimize – not to inhibit or repress. It proves so effective because it does not operate by means of forbidding and depriving, but by pleasing and fulfilling. Instead of making people compliant, it seeks to make them dependent.

According to Deleuze, the disciplinary regime organizes itself as a ‘body’. It is a biopolitical regime. The neoliberal regime, in contrast, seems like a ‘soul’.2 As such, psychopolitics is its form of government: it is ‘constantly introducing an inexorable rivalry presented as healthy competition … wonderful motivation’.3 Motivation, projects, competition, optimization and initiative represent features of the psychopolitical technology of domination that constitutes the neoliberal regime.
Disciplinary power is normative power. It subjects the subject to a set of rules – norms, commandments and prohibitions – and eliminates deviations and anomalies.

But neoliberalism, a further development – indeed, a mutated form – of capitalism, is not primarily concerned with ‘the biological, the somatic, the corporal’. It has discovered the psyche as a productive force. This psychic turn – that is, the turn to psychopolitics – also connects with the mode of operation of contemporary capitalism. Now, immaterial and non-physical forms of production are what determine the course of capitalism. What gets produced are not material objects, but immaterial ones – for instance, information and programs. The body no longer represents a central force of production, as it formerly did in biopolitical, disciplinary society. Now, productivity is not to be enhanced by overcoming physical resistance so much as by optimizing psychic or mental processes. Physical discipline has given way to mental optimization. And neuro-enhancement differs from the disciplinary techniques of psychiatry fundamentally.

Today, the body is being released from the immediate process of production and turning into the object of optimization, whether along aesthetic lines or in terms of health technology. Accordingly, orthopaedic intervention is yielding to aesthetic intervention. Foucault’s ‘docile body’ has no place in this production process. Cosmetic surgery and fitness studios are taking the place of disciplinary orthopaedics. That said, physical optimization means more than aesthetic practice alone: sexiness and fitness represent new economic resources to be increased, marketed and exploited.

Foucault did not see that the neoliberal regime utterly claims the technology of the self for its own purposes: perpetual self-optimization – as the exemplary neoliberal technology of the self – represents nothing so much as a highly efficient mode of domination and exploitation.12 As an ‘entrepreneur of himself’,13 the neoliberal achievement-subject engages in auto-exploitation willingly – and even passionately. The self-as-a-work-of-art amounts to a beautiful but deceptive illusion that the neoliberal regime maintains in order to exhaust its resources entirely.

The neoliberal imperative of self-optimization serves only to promote perfect functioning within the system. Inhibitions, points of weakness and mistakes are to be therapeutically eliminated in order to enhance efficiency and performance. In turn, everything is made comparable and measurable and subjected to the logic of the market. It is not concern for the good life that drives self-optimization. Rather, self-optimization follows from systemic constraints – from the logic of quantifying success on the market.
